question: What is the primary organ responsible for eliminating water-soluble drugs from the body?
explanation: The kidneys specialize in filtering and excreting water-soluble drugs and metabolic waste products through urine. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why are gases like inhaled anesthetics mainly breathed out through the lungs?

options.A: They are too large to pass through the kidneys
options.B: They must first be turned into solids by the lungs
options.C: They push open special pumps in the tiny airways
options.D: They easily cross the tiny air sacs into the breath

explanation: Volatile substances easily cross the thin alveolar membrane from the blood into the air in the lungs to be breathed out. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h1)

question: Which type of drug molecules can pass through the kidney's tiny filtering units?

options.D: Drugs that are unbound and free

explanation: Only free, unbound drugs that are small enough to fit through the tiny capillary pores can enter the kidney's filtering system. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h2)

question: For a drug to stay trapped in the kidney tubes and be passed out in urine, what property must it have?
explanation: Polar and ionized molecules cannot easily cross cell membranes back into the blood, so they stay in the urine to be eliminated. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h2)

question: How does making a patient's urine more alkaline affect weak acid medications?

options.A: It neutralizes them so they are quickly reabsorbed into the blood
options.B: It binds them to proteins to stop kidney filtration
options.C: It turns them into fat-soluble compounds that stay in the body
options.D: It ionizes them so they cannot be reabsorbed and leave the body faster

explanation: Alkaline urine turns weak acids into their charged, ionized form, trapping them in the kidney tubes so they are quickly passed out. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h3)

question: Why do older adults often need lower doses of drugs that are cleared by the kidneys?

options.A: Their liver enzymes break down drugs faster
options.B: Their kidney filtering rate naturally declines with age
options.C: Their active kidney secretion works much faster
options.D: They produce more proteins in their blood

explanation: Aging causes a natural reduction in kidney function, which lowers the filtering rate and slows down how fast drugs leave the body. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h3)

question: Where do drugs that are excreted through the biliary system eventually end up?
explanation: Bile flows from the liver into the biliary tract and empties directly into the lumen of the small intestine. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h4)

question: What happens when a drug goes through enterohepatic recirculation in the body?

options.A: It prevents the drug from ever reaching the liver
options.B: It stays active in the body longer by being reabsorbed from the gut
options.C: It turns fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble ions instantly
options.D: It immediately clears the drug from the bloodstream

explanation: By reabsorbing the drug back into the bloodstream from the digestive tract, enterohepatic cycling keeps the medication working in the body longer. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h4)

question: Which way of eliminating drugs from the body can pose a direct risk to a nursing infant?
explanation: Fat-soluble drugs easily pass into breast milk, meaning a nursing infant can swallow active medication. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why does the alcohol in a person's breath match the level of alcohol in their blood?

options.A: Alcohol passes freely from blood vessels into the air sacs of the lungs
options.B: Alcohol is actively pumped out through the airways
options.C: Saliva glands push alcohol into the mouth during breathing
options.D: Inhaled oxygen breaks down blood alcohol into gas

explanation: Alcohol acts like a volatile gas that crosses easily across the membrane between the lung capillaries and air sacs, allowing blood levels to be measured from breath. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h5)

question: What does a drug's half-life mean in clinical practice?

options.A: The time it takes for the drug to be fully absorbed
options.B: The time it takes for the drug level in the blood to drop by half
options.C: The time it takes to feel the strongest effect of the drug
options.D: The time liver enzymes need to activate the drug

explanation: Half-life is simply the time it takes for the concentration of a medication in the bloodstream to reduce by fifty percent. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h6)

question: How does severe kidney failure affect a drug's elimination half-life?

options.A: It leaves the half-life completely unchanged
options.B: It makes the half-life shorter because the liver works harder
options.C: It stops drug breakdown in the stomach entirely
options.D: It makes the half-life longer because the drug leaves the body slower

explanation: When kidney clearance drops, the body eliminates the drug much slower, which stretches out its half-life in the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which lab test do nurses usually check to see how well a patient's kidneys are clearing drugs?
explanation: Serum creatinine levels and calculated creatinine clearance are the main clinical guides nurses use to check kidney filtering function. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why do nurses closely monitor patients with kidney problems who are taking drugs cleared by the kidneys?

options.A: To prevent the drug from building up to toxic levels in the body
options.B: To make sure the drug turns into fat stores quickly
options.C: To stop the kidneys from losing body proteins
options.D: To speed up drug movement through the gut

explanation: When kidney excretion is slow, drugs can build up in the blood to dangerous levels, making close monitoring essential to prevent toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T4#GNS125_U5_T4_h7)
